spots.name: Patong Beach
spots.label: Patong Beach

text.geographic_location: Patong is on the west coast of Phuket, in the island's main tourist resort area. The beach runs along the western edge of the town. The Patong Beach Viewpoint is listed on Thawewong Road, a hillside road above the beach, so check the exact spot on the map.
text.directions_text: No railway station or tram stop is listed near this spot. From there, Patong Beach is about 960 m to the south (roughly 15 minutes on foot). The Patong Beach Viewpoint is listed on Thawewong Road, so check the exact spot on the map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description:
Patong is the busiest beach resort on Phuket's west coast, and its long, curving beach runs the whole length of the town's western side, roughly 2.85 km (1.77 miles) end to end. It became popular with Western visitors in the late 1980s and has grown into the island's main tourist resort, with many hotels and the centre of its shopping and nightlife. The town was hit hard by the tsunami of 26 December 2004, but it has largely recovered.

The best phone view is from above rather than from the sand. That height lets you fit the whole sweep of the bay into one frame, which is hard to do at ground level. Sunset is the moment to aim for, when the scene warms up and the lights start to come on along the front.

There is also a lot to see once you walk down to the beach. Umbrellas, sunbathers and boats make good small scenes, and the evening crowds add life to your shots. If you want a second angle, the hillside viewpoints at Wat Doi Thepnimit and Kalim both look back over Patong Bay. Kalim is quieter and reached by road.
text.access_note: The viewpoint is listed as free; check local signs before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset colours don't wash out. After the sun has gone, switch to night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep the lights sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole curve of the bay, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details on the beach below, such as umbrellas, boats or people on the sand.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line where the sand meets the sea along the lower third, leaving the sky and the water as the rest of the frame. Keep the horizon level. Try a slow panorama to sweep along the bay, or zoom in for a closer shot of one busy patch of beach. For a different angle, the viewpoints at Wat Doi Thepnimit and Kalim also overlook the bay.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the light warms up and the lights below start to come on. Go a little early to find a good spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Patong Beach Viewpoint (on Thawewong Road, the road that runs along the hill above the beach). An elevated panorama where the town meets the sea, with the beach and its activity visible below. The beach and the town's activity are laid out below you.

spots.name: Phuket Old Town
spots.label: Phuket Old Town

text.geographic_location: Phuket Old Town is an area of historical interest in the city of Phuket. Its main streets are Thalang, Phang Nga, Krabi, Dibuk and Yoawarat.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed nearby, so start from Phuket Town and walk to the phone icon on the map. Walk west for about 6 minutes on foot to reach its streets. The phone icon on the map is about 370 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description:
Phuket Old Town is the historic part of Phuket Town, and it photographs well because the streets are lined on both sides with Sino-Portuguese buildings. The main streets are Thalang, Phang Nga, Krabi, Dibuk and Yoawarat. Many of the old shophouses and mansions have become shops, hotels, restaurants and museums, so there is usually something to frame in the foreground, such as a doorway, a sign or a café table.

The area grew rich on tin mining. Hokkien Chinese miners did much of the work in the 18th century and helped build the old part of the city. In the early 20th century, roads and canals were built and European mining companies were invited in. Many buildings from that time have been preserved and restored. The area is also tied to the Baba community, which came from early unions between Hokkien tin-miners and Siamese women.

For your phone, think in rows and repeats. Repeating shopfronts and arches make good leading lines down a street. Close detail shots, such as window shutters, tiled floors and door carvings, work as well as wide views. Walk slowly and look up, because the upper floors are often the most interesting part. Stand at a corner to catch two streets in one frame, and keep an eye on traffic when you step back to compose.
text.access_note: The streets are open public space, but individual museums, shops and restaurants have their own rules, so check the official site before you go to any of them.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so bright walls keep their colour. Use portrait mode if you photograph a person in front of a shopfront.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for whole street scenes, then switch to the default lens (1x) for shopfronts. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for upper-floor details and signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the rows of shophouses so the verticals stay straight. Use the street as a leading line towards a distant corner. Keep a doorway or signboard in the foreground for depth. Then take a few close-ups of decorative details with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the streets are likely to be quieter and the light softer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 370 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Take your main photos there, on the pavement at a street corner.

spots.name: Phuket Thai Hua Museum
spots.label: Thai Hua Museum

text.geographic_location: In Phuket Old Town, on Krabi Road, a quiet side street just east of Thalang Road.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, train or tram stops near here, so start from Thalang Road in Phuket Old Town and head east onto Krabi Road. Navigate to Krabi Road, just east of Thalang Road. The museum is on the street itself, so you can photograph the front as soon as you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description:
Phuket Thai Hua Museum sits in a 1934 mansion in Phuket Old Town, and its front is the reason to stop with a phone in hand. The two-storey Sino-Portuguese facade has an arched entrance, shuttered windows and decorative plasterwork, and together they make a tidy, colourful composition that suits a straight-on shot. The museum is on Krabi Road, a quiet side street just east of Thalang Road, so it is easy to pair with a stroll through the old town.

The front facade is the main photo point. The outside of the building can be photographed from the street without going in, which makes it an easy quick stop. Interior photography may need a separate pass, so check opening days before you go if you plan to shoot inside.

For a first picture, stand in front of the entrance and centre the arch, using the gridlines to keep the shutters and walls upright. Then move in for a close shot of the plasterwork around the windows and doorway. For something calmer than the busy front, look for the quieter, older-looking corner at the back of the museum, where old roof tiles are stacked. It gives a more weathered, textured picture and makes a good second frame. Morning or late afternoon is the time one guide suggests for exterior photos.
text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but interior photography and opening days may vary, so check opening days before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out, or up if the shaded front looks dark. Wipe the lens first, as street dust can soften the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit both storeys, and use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the plasterwork and shutters.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the arch and turn on the gridlines so the walls and shutters stay straight. Hold the phone level and keep it at chest height to limit leaning verticals. Then zoom in on the plasterwork for a detail shot. For a different picture, try the quieter back corner of the museum with the stacked old roof tiles in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, according to one guide, for exterior photos.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back onto the street in front of พิพิธภัณฑ์ภูเก็ตไทยหัว, facing the front facade on Krabi Road, so you can fit the whole front in. From there you see the whole Sino-Portuguese front with its arched entrance and shuttered windows.
